title: Responsible by Design: Evaluating and Testing AI Tools for Accuracy and Reliability — TRI/NCSC AI Policy Consortium webinar 25
pub: TRI/NCSC AI Policy Consortium for Law & Courts (Thomson Reuters Institute / National Center for State Courts) — monthly webinar series, webinar 25
author: Angela Tripp · Keith Porcaro · Margaret Hagan

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts selective, use-context-specific deployment and materially extends it with a court-focused operating framework: representative testing, independent oversight, staged approval, continuous post-launch evaluation, and authority to rescope or terminate. It also concretely differentiates the controls required for bounded internal tools from higher-risk public-facing systems.
qs: To validate it for your use case, you needed to test it on data that resembles your users.
When you get those changes, when you see a change, that's when you need to retest your entire sort of suite again.

kp.k: Court AI requires institution-owned evaluation, not vendor assurances
kp.d: Angela Tripp frames the webinar around accuracy and reliability of internal and public-facing court AI, including self-help, filing triage, translation, transcription, forms assembly and research assistance. Margaret Hagan argues that frontline experts and court leaders must define quality and authorize deployment because they bear the consequences; technical teams may implement evaluation but should not own these judgments. These are practitioner recommendations rather than findings from a reported study.
qs: When we talk about evaluation today, it is in the context of whether a tool can reliably return accurate results.
this has to rest with the frontline experts, the court leaders, the subject matter experts about what is green-lighted and what quality looks like.
And then you can delegate back to a technology or research team to implement that evaluation.

kp.k: Testing shifts project costs beyond initial software construction
kp.d: Keith Porcaro argues that connecting a model through an API and building an interface can be relatively inexpensive, while repeated refinement and testing consume substantial time, staffing and money. His $30,000 launch and three-month timeline example illustrates an inadequate vendor pitch, not a measured project cost. Three months may suffice for a very simple project with existing infrastructure, but he expects complex and public-facing projects to take much longer. He recommends dedicated evaluation platforms rather than document-based workflows at scale.
qs: What really is going to take up time and money here are the cycles of refinement and testing that you're going to need to do
Doing this in Google Docs, doing this in Word documents is just not going to cut it at scale.
three months might be enough for a very, very simple project, especially if you have this infrastructure already ready to go.
But most projects, especially complex projects, especially projects that are public-facing, are going to take much longer.

kp.k: Usage and satisfaction cannot establish legal accuracy
kp.d: Porcaro warns that visitor counts include bots and superficial engagement, while feedback is sparse and selectively submitted. He illustrates that thousands of sessions might yield only a couple dozen ratings, without presenting a defined dataset. Self-help users may approve persuasive misinformation or reject correct but unwelcome advice. Hagan and Porcaro nevertheless recommend feedback and focused usability testing as complementary evidence about accessibility, intent and usefulness, not substitutes for accuracy evaluation.
qs: Here, for you, a data set with thousands of sessions might have a couple dozen thumbs up and thumbs down, which just isn't enough to get anything meaningful out of it.
They might give a thumbs down to an answer that is correct but is not what they wanted to hear. They might give a thumbs up to something that looks really persuasive but is completely wrong.
I would say it's a helpful signal, but an incomplete one.

kp.k: Approved-content retrieval does not eliminate errors
kp.d: Porcaro rejects claims that retrieval-augmented generation is safe by default. Retrieval can omit relevant material, select irrelevant excerpts or combine unrelated documents, producing incorrect answers despite correct source content. Users unfamiliar with legal terminology may phrase questions differently from the resources, increasing difficulties for public-facing tools. He also identifies imperfect instruction-following as a risk and reports that his lab's RAG audits encounter errors, without giving sample sizes or measured rates.
qs: Any of those can generate wrong answers, even if all of your content is correct.
RAG also relies on sort of another bet, that the people who are using the tool write in a way that is similar to the people who wrote the resources.
My lab audits RAG tools all the time. They are never error-free.

kp.k: Demos need repeated testing with representative local inputs
kp.d: Porcaro argues that nondeterminism and sensitivity to small input changes make polished demonstrations unreliable guides to deployment performance. He reports observing nearly identical questions receiving opposite substantive answers, without quantifying frequency. He recommends validation using local emails, support requests or staff inputs. Hagan adds repeated runs, institution-selected cases, high-risk scenarios and evaluation by people other than the builders, including for open-source tools adopted from other courts.
qs: when you give a model the same input twice, you might actually get different outputs each time.
So two people can ask nearly identical questions and get opposite substantive answers.
To validate it for your use case, you needed to test it on data that resembles your users.
You want to make sure that it's being tested with that same rigor and by people who are not the ones who built it.

kp.k: Initial approval requires explicit objectives and harm boundaries
kp.d: Hagan proposes three evaluation phases: initial project approval, development toward a pilot, and ongoing maintenance. Before committing resources, leaders should specify three to five organizational or user outcomes, concrete tasks, quality rubrics, representative test cases and unacceptable harms. They should demand that builders explain failure modes and decide whether to proceed, narrow scope, retest in six months or decline. These are governance recommendations, not a guarantee that prohibited harms can be eliminated.
qs: That should be three to five items about improving your organization or your users or your staff's experience.
What are those examples that you would want a technical system to be able to handle? You should also be very explicit about what are the harms.
If they don't and they say their system has no failure modes, that's a big red flag.
Maybe we'll retest in six months, but we're not ready to go there yet.

kp.k: Prelaunch refinement involves regressions and accountable trade-offs
kp.d: Porcaro describes development as a 'hill climb' involving model choice, prompts, query processing, resource chunking and answer scope. Improvements are not linear: changes may improve one area while degrading another. He recommends largely settled rubrics for comparable test runs, minimally interpretive criteria and institution-owned resolution of disagreements. Builders may otherwise favor easier implementation rather than the court's substantive priorities.
qs: You might improve one area and cause a regression in another area.
That's why it's so important to have your rubrics and your criteria largely settled before you start to do this
your rubric criteria as you're building it should be as objective and sort of minimally interpretive as possible.
The risk of putting it onto technical teams or onto vendors or onto builders is that they're going to default to what makes the project easier for them to build.

kp.k: Deployment creates continuing evaluation and contractual obligations
kp.d: Porcaro recommends regularly sampling real user sessions for human and automated evaluation, adding newly observed failures to test cases and monitoring abuse or guardrail circumvention. Post-launch testing may be less intensive than development, but model or product changes require rerunning the entire test suite, including changes described as bug fixes. Courts should incorporate this work into vendor contracts and ongoing budgets.
qs: But you should be regularly sampling real user sessions and running human and then automated evals on them.
AI models shift, products change. When you get those changes, when you see a change, that's when you need to retest your entire sort of suite again.
You need to build all of this into your vendor contract, and you need to factor it into your ongoing cost model.

kp.k: Incident governance must precede public deployment
kp.d: Porcaro advises defining who can stop, modify or continue a tool before problems arise. Written arrangements should establish vendor response times, responsibility for retesting costs and public notification for sufficiently serious problems. Tripp adds that institutions need both decision authority and the practical capacity to take a tool offline quickly. The speakers present these as preparedness measures, not claims that every deployment will experience severe harm.
qs: Before a problem comes up, before you launch, is when you need to set the sort of governance for the ongoing maintenance of your tool down.
You need to establish turnaround expectations in writing for your vendor or your builder team in your court.
If you need to do a whole round of new testing in order to validate that a fix has actually been implemented, who's paying for that?
And in the rare instance that a problem is bad enough, you need to decide how the public is notified.

kp.k: Audience, inputs and task breadth determine evaluation burden
kp.d: Hagan argues that trained internal users, bounded inputs and discrete tasks with knowable answers make evaluation more manageable than public access, unrestricted uploads and broad conversational assistance. For public-facing tools with unstructured input, she recommends thousands of test cases and hundreds of staff-review hours per quarter, alongside substantial development and maintenance budgets. These are planning recommendations rather than documented costs or staffing observations.
qs: Just it's much more manageable to control the staff-facing things versus the public, shorthand.
Obviously, it takes a lot more testing and a much larger data set of examples to then test when you're having that Swiss Army knife kind of platform.
You need to have thousands of test cases, you need to be planning for hundreds of hours per quarter of staff reviewing this

kp.k: Document extraction and self-help chatbots need different controls
kp.d: Hagan contrasts two illustrative court projects rather than reporting completed deployments. Internal extraction into case-management systems requires sample documents, ground-truth fields, testing against handwriting and blurry images, and post-launch sampling with alerts for pipeline changes. An unrestricted public chatbot requires broader scenarios, explicit harm boundaries, months of iterative correction and conversation review that can identify missing content, user misunderstandings or reasons to withdraw the tool.
qs: In phase two, you're going to have to make sure that that AI system works accurately, even if there's handwriting or blurry images, other problems.
Phase three, after you've launched it, you want to be watching that system and maybe sample documents weekly, like Keith was saying.
you're keeping a bugs list of, oh, we changed it for here, but then that made it answer wrong over here.
You need to be having staff and possibly AI as judges watching and reviewing the conversations.

kp.k: Multilingual tools require additional expertise, not assumed thresholds
kp.d: Asked whether tools serving limited-English-proficient litigants should face a higher accuracy bar, Hagan and Porcaro leave acceptable error rates to organizational leadership rather than supplying a benchmark. Porcaro recommends expertise to validate other-language offerings and additional checks on appropriate legal terminology, beyond substantive legal correctness, because users may lack terms of art in either language.
qs: I think it is ultimately a leadership question.
you need to source the expertise for validating that offerings in other languages are actually going to work
you might be analyzing sort of appropriate uses of terms of art in the non-English language

kp.k: Expert-supervised pilots can precede access by junior users
kp.d: Hagan describes a current development approach that first targets highly experienced practitioners who can recognize and reject errors. Her example of saving time on 75% of uses while experts reject errors in the other 25% is illustrative, not a measured productivity or error finding. She proposes progressively extending access to junior staff, volunteers, community navigators and potentially the public as performance improves. The mechanism depends on human expertise and checking, not autonomous reliance on outputs.
qs: there's always a trained professional who knows this practice inside and out and can flag major error, but they can still get some value out of it.
It might save them time on 75% of the times they use it, and the other 25% there's errors, they see those errors immediately and they reject that.
And then we might expand out to gradually let more junior people use it who might not be able to spot the errors as much
but not aiming for general public users in our first pilot.

kp.k: Funding and publicity should accommodate unsuccessful experiments
kp.d: Porcaro recommends structuring AI projects as staged experiments with permission to change scope or stop, rather than promising a launch. He suggests negotiating this with funders early and sharing criteria and testing evidence as work proceeds. His observation that some organizations are slowing adoption is explicitly anecdotal. Tripp warns against announcing success based on a demonstration or another jurisdiction's adoption before evaluation or audit.
qs: it's important to structure these projects like the experiments that they are
this is not a promise that this tool is going to be actually capable of launch. This is a hypothesis for what we think is going to happen.
Do not write your success story before doing an evaluation or audit.
We have to get more comfortable with intelligent failures or intelligent rescoping.

kp.k: Courts need internal technical expertise independent of builders
kp.d: Tripp recommends an internal expert who understands evaluation protocols and measurement and can build assets for continuing assessment, working for the institution rather than its vendor or build team. Leaders should ask which cases underpin error rates, who scored them, whether scorers agreed, what failures occurred and who authorized system rules. This creates an institutional oversight role without requiring every court leader to become an AI engineer.
qs: That person needs to work for you, not a vendor or the team building the tool.
What was the error rate on which cases and who scored them? Did two different scorers agree with each other?
Show me the 20 cases that it got wrong so that you can look at them and understand what kinds of errors are happening.
What rules are built into this system, and who signed off on them?

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The speakers describe court and legal-aid AI deployment as an ongoing experimental service-development process, with substantial testing costs, audience-dependent risks, and more immediately manageable opportunities for expert-assisted internal work than unrestricted public self-help.
pts.d: 1. Keith Porcaro claims that AI makes prototypes easier to build, but leaves a substantial gap between a persuasive demonstration and production readiness. Relative to traditional custom software, initial development can account for less of the budget, while repeated testing and refinement consume much of the work and money. 2. Porcaro claims that retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) using approved legal content is not safe by default: retrieval can omit relevant material, select misleading excerpts, or combine unrelated documents, and the model can depart from instructions. Users unfamiliar with legal terminology face particular difficulties. 3. Porcaro claims that generative systems' variable outputs and sensitivity to inputs mean that a successful vendor demonstration does not establish fitness for a court's own users. Refinement is not reliably linear: fixing one problem can worsen another. 4. Porcaro and Margaret Hagan claim that visitor counts and positive user feedback cannot establish legal accuracy or absence of harm. Users may approve persuasive but incorrect answers, dislike correct answers, or leave without reporting a bad experience. Hagan adds that adverse consequences may emerge after an initially positive interaction. 5. Hagan claims that testing demands depend heavily on scope: internal tools with controlled inputs and discrete, objectively checkable tasks are more manageable than public-facing, open-input, multipurpose tools. For the latter, she advises planning thousands of test cases and hundreds of staff-review hours per quarter. 6. Porcaro, Hagan and Angela Tripp argue that deployed AI requires continuing evaluation, including sampling actual use, identifying new failure modes and retesting after changes. They assign court leadership responsibility for quality standards, risk acceptance and decisions to change or discontinue a service rather than leaving those decisions to vendors. 7. Hagan proposes expert-first deployment as a practical route to value: experienced practitioners may save time even with imperfect tools because they can identify and reject erroneous outputs. Expansion to juniors, volunteers, community navigators and the public should follow demonstrated improvement rather than precede it. 8. Porcaro says non-English legal assistance requires validation not only of legal substance but also of appropriate terminology and user understanding. Neither he nor Hagan supplies a universal acceptable error rate. 9. Porcaro reports anecdotal signs that some organizations are becoming more cautious as concrete harms become visible; he expresses hope, rather than a demonstrated finding, that this will increase rigor.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The claims principally rest on the speakers' auditing, building and advisory experience, supported by technical explanations and illustrative scenarios—not reported controlled studies, named benchmark results or documented quantitative outcome estimates.
pts.d: Porcaro grounds claims about unreliable RAG outputs, input sensitivity, evaluation failures and deployment costs in Duke's audits of court and legal-aid tools and conversations with organizations undertaking AI projects. He explains mechanisms that can produce errors, but gives no named audited product, sample size, measured error rate or published audit result. Hagan grounds her scope and deployment recommendations in hands-on building and early-stage R&D with courts and legal-aid organizations, including student projects. The contrast between document-field extraction and a general self-help chatbot is illustrative, not a comparative study of two identified deployments. Her thousands-of-tests and hundreds-of-review-hours estimates are planning guidance without an accompanying calculation. The 75% time-saving-use / 25% erroneous-use scenario illustrates possible value under expert verification; it is not presented as measured productivity or accuracy data. Likewise, Porcaro's visitor-conversion and feedback-volume figures illustrate why usage metrics can be misleading, rather than supplying a documented dataset. Claims about growing caution are explicitly anecdotal. Tripp's governance and staffing conclusions are recommendations drawn from the presentation, not empirical findings. The transcript does not establish that these tools improve litigant outcomes or close the justice gap.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: These are present-tense assessments in a 2026 webinar and conditional deployment expectations, organized around initial approval, pre-launch refinement and ongoing operation, rather than dated forecasts of profession-wide transformation.
pts.d: Porcaro says three months might suffice for a very simple project when evaluation infrastructure already exists, but complex and especially public-facing projects usually need longer. Hagan describes public-chatbot refinement as work continuing for many months and its review burden as recurring quarterly. Post-launch evaluation can be less intensive than pre-launch testing, but should continue regularly; model or product changes trigger renewed full-suite testing. Lower testing demands are conditional on constrained tasks and inputs, trained internal users, and organizational oversight—not an assertion that internal tools are error-free. Hagan's expert-first pathway depends on genuinely experienced users being able to detect major errors, and later expansion depends on the tool improving enough for less expert users. She presents gradual expansion as a working theory, not a guaranteed trajectory or scheduled rollout. For multilingual services, acceptable risk remains an organizational leadership decision requiring relevant expertise. Porcaro emphasizes that an AI project is a hypothesis whose scope may change or whose development may stop; launching a service is not assured merely because development receives funding.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are court leaders and staff, legal-aid practitioners, self-represented and non-English-speaking litigants, and the builders and funders supporting these services.
pts.d: Court leaders acquire continuing responsibilities for defining acceptable quality, allocating review resources, resolving trade-offs, and authorizing shutdowns or scope changes. Tripp recommends access to a technically knowledgeable internal evaluation expert independent of the vendor or build team. Court staff and experienced legal-aid practitioners are potential beneficiaries of narrowly scoped assistance, including extracting case-document fields and supporting established legal workflows, but their human checking remains essential to the expert-first model. Junior practitioners, volunteers and community navigators are possible later users with less ability to spot errors, so Hagan does not treat their readiness as equivalent to that of experienced lawyers. Self-represented litigants using public self-help systems face risks from incorrect, generic or misunderstood information and may be unable to assess answer quality; their satisfaction is therefore not a substitute for substantive evaluation. Non-English-speaking litigants face additional terminology and misunderstanding risks requiring suitable validation expertise. Vendors and technical teams face requirements for evaluation infrastructure, change notification, remediation and agreed cost allocation, while funders are asked to accommodate experimental outcomes, including non-launch. The webinar does not predict lawyer headcount reductions, changes to firm leverage or billing models, or measurable legal-market displacement.
